entry:
Raised structure that juts out from a shore over a body of water, usually supported by piles or pillars. Piers provide above-water access to offshore areas for [[Fishing|fishing]], [[Boat|boat]] docking, the loading of passengers and [[Cargo|cargo]], and oceanside recreation. Their open structure lets tides and currents flow relatively unhindered. Piers range from simple lightweight wooden structures to major structures extended over 1,600 m (5,200 ft).

The term has regional nuances. In [[North America]] and [[Australia]], where many ports were built on the multiple pier model until recently, it usually implies a current or former cargo-handling facility. In Europe, where ports more often use basins and river-side quays, it is principally associated with the Victorian [[Cast iron|cast iron]] pleasure pier that emerged in Great Britain in the early 19th century. In American English, a pier may be synonymous with a [[Dock|dock]].

Italian poet, writer, and film director, known for *The Gospel According to St. Matthew* and *Salò, or the 120 Days of Sodom*. Openly homosexual, he became an avowed Marxist after [[World War II]] and remained a controversial figure whose legacy is contentious. His films combined socio-political polemic with graphic examination of [[Taboo|taboo]] sexual activity. He was a prominent figure of the [[Rome]] intellectual scene in the postwar era. He was murdered at Ostia in November 1975, and the killing prompted an outcry in Italy. Recent leads by cold case investigators suggest a contract killing by the Banda della Magliana, a criminal organization.

Irish actor and film producer. He achieved worldwide fame playing [[James Bond (literary character)|James Bond]] in four films from 1995 to 2002. He rose to popularity in the television series *Remington Steele* (1982–1987), and his films include *The Lawnmower Man* (1992), *Mrs. Doubtfire* (1993), and *Mamma Mia!* (2008). In 1996 he and American film producer Beau St. Clair founded the production company Irish DreamTime. He received a star on the [[Hollywood Walk of Fame]] in 1997 for his contributions to the film industry, and he is known for charitable work and environmental activism.

Butterfly in the family Pieridae, also called the large white or cabbage butterfly. It is a close relative of the small white, *Pieris rapae*, and is common throughout Europe, North Africa, and Asia to the [[Himalayas|Himalayas]], often in agricultural areas, meadows, and parkland. The wings are white with black tips on the forewings, and the wingspan reaches 5 to 6.5 cm on average. [[Larva|Larvae]] go through four [[Moulting|moultings]] and five instars, and the third instar causes significant damage to host plants. The species established a population in South Africa. In 2010 it was found in Nelson, New Zealand, where it was classed as an unwanted pest. After a public capture campaign and over 263,000 searches, it was officially declared eradicated from New Zealand as of December 2014.

Filled dumpling, a traditional Polish dish made by wrapping unleavened dough around a filling and boiling it. Typical fillings include potato and tvorog cheese, sauerkraut, ground meat, mushrooms, fruit, or berries, and savory pierogi are often served with sour cream or fried onions. The recipe dates back to at least 1682, when Poland's first cookbook, *Compendium ferculorum, albo Zebranie potraw*, was published. The Polish word is the plural of *pieróg*, derived from Proto-Slavic *pirъ*, meaning "feast". Some claim that [[Marco Polo]] spread the dumplings along the [[Silk Road]], suggesting a link to Chinese *mantou*, but their origin is unknown and debated. Pierogi are also popular in [[Canada]] and the [[United States]].

French [[Impressionism|Impressionist]] painter. Born in [[Limoges]], he left school at thirteen to apprentice at a porcelain factory, then studied art in Paris under Charles Gleyre, where he met [[Claude Monet]]. Inspired by [[Camille Pissarro]] and [[Édouard Manet]], he joined the First Impressionist Exhibition in 1874, displaying six paintings. After a trip to Italy in 1881 he adopted a more structured style influenced by [[Raphael]] and Rubens. From the 1890s severe rheumatism led him to settle in Cagnes-sur-Mer in southern France, where he produced monumental nudes and still lifes. His son [[Jean Renoir]] became a filmmaker. Renoir's depiction of feminine beauty and his optimistic celebration of human connection influenced later artists, including Pablo Picasso and Henri Matisse.

French composer, conductor, and writer, one of the dominant figures of post-war [[Contemporary classical music|contemporary classical music]]. He studied at the Conservatoire de Paris with Olivier Messiaen and played an important role in the development of integral serialism in the 1950s, controlled chance music in the 1960s, and the electronic transformation of instrumental music from the 1970s. Because he revised earlier compositions, his body of work is relatively small, but it includes landmarks such as *Le Marteau sans maître*, *Pli selon pli*, and *Répons*. As a conductor he was music director of the New York Philharmonic and chief conductor of the BBC Symphony Orchestra. He founded the Domaine musical in Paris in the 1950s and established IRCAM in the 1970s. Some critics called his uncompromising modernism dogmatic.

French sociologist and public intellectual. His work concerned the dynamics of power in society and how social order is maintained across generations, stressing the role of practice and embodiment in social life. Building on and criticizing [[Karl Marx]], [[Sigmund Freud]], [[Max Weber]], and [[Émile Durkheim]], he introduced concepts including cultural reproduction, habitus, field, symbolic violence, and cultural, social, and symbolic capital. His best-known book, *Distinction: A Social Critique of the Judgment of Taste* (1979), argues that judgments of taste are acts of social positioning. He argued that the ruling and intellectual classes preserve their privileges across generations despite what he called a myth of equal opportunity in post-industrial society. During the [[Algerian War]] (1958–1962) he undertook ethnographic research into the conflict.

French physicist and chemist, a pioneer in [[Crystallography|crystallography]] and magnetism. In 1880 he and his brother Jacques demonstrated that an electric potential is generated when crystals are compressed, a phenomenon known as [[Piezoelectricity|piezoelectricity]]. He studied [[Ferromagnetism|ferromagnetism]], paramagnetism, and diamagnetism, and discovered the effect of temperature on paramagnetism, now known as Curie's law. He also identified the critical temperature above which ferromagnetic substances lose their ferromagnetic behavior, now called the Curie temperature. With his wife, [[Marie Curie]], he worked on isolating [[Polonium|polonium]] and [[Radium|radium]], and they were the first to use the term radioactivity. He shared half of the 1903 [[Nobel Prize|Nobel Prize]] in Physics with his wife, making them the first married couple to win a Nobel Prize.

French [[Anarchism|anarchist]], socialist, and economist, considered by many the "father of anarchism". A printer who taught himself Latin, he founded mutualist philosophy and was the first person known to self-identify as an anarchist. His 1840 book *What Is Property?* declared that "property is theft!", attracting the attention of the French authorities and of [[Karl Marx]]. Their friendship ended over *The Poverty of Philosophy*, a dispute that became one source of the split between anarchist and Marxist wings of the International Working Men's Association. Proudhon favored workers' cooperatives and individual possession over private ownership or nationalization of land and workplaces, and he considered social revolution achievable peacefully. He sat in the French Parliament after the Revolution of 1848, and his attempt to create a national bank offering interest-free loans failed. After the death of [[Mikhail Bakunin]], his libertarian socialism diverged into several anarchist strands, including those of [[Peter Kropotkin]].

French polymath and marquis whose work was instrumental in physics, astronomy, mathematics, and statistics. In his five-volume *Mécanique céleste* (1799–1825) he summarized and extended the work of his predecessors, translating the geometric study of mechanics into one based on [[Calculus|calculus]]. In statistics, the Bayesian interpretation of probability was developed mainly by Laplace. He pioneered the [[Laplace transform|Laplace transform]] and restated and developed the [[Nebular hypothesis|nebular hypothesis]] of the origin of the [[Solar System|Solar System]]. He refined [[Isaac Newton|Newton]]'s calculation of the [[Speed of sound|speed of sound]] and was one of the first scientists to suggest an idea similar to a [[Black hole|black hole]]. He originated Laplace's demon, a hypothetical all-predicting intellect. He examined [[Napoleon]] when Napoleon graduated from the École Militaire in Paris in 1785.

Canadian lawyer and politician, prime minister of Canada (1968–1979; 1980–1984). As Liberal leader he pioneered official bilingualism and [[Multiculturalism|multiculturalism]]. As justice minister from 1967 to 1968 he liberalized divorce and abortion laws and decriminalized homosexuality. Facing the [[Quebec|Quebec]] sovereignty movement, he invoked the War Measures Act during the 1970 October Crisis, and he later led the federalist campaign to victory in the 1980 Quebec referendum. He introduced a capital gains [[Tax|tax]], established Petro-Canada, and launched the National Energy Program, which increased Western alienation. In foreign policy he developed strong ties with [[Cuba|Cuba]] and its leader [[Fidel Castro|Fidel Castro]], and he oversaw Canada's entry into the [[G7|G7]]. In 1982 he enacted the Constitution Act, which patriated the constitution and established the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Critics accused him of arrogance and economic mismanagement, while admirers praised his intellect. His son, [[Justin Trudeau]], later served as prime minister.

French educator and historian, co-founder of the International Olympic Committee and father of the modern [[Olympic Games|Olympic Games]]. Born into a French aristocratic family, he studied education and history and was particularly active in promoting sport in French schools. He came up with the idea of reviving the Olympic Games while at the Paris Institute of Political Studies (Sciences Po). Coubertin grew up amid the [[Franco-Prussian War|Franco-Prussian War]] and the [[Paris Commune|Paris Commune]]. As a boarder at a Jesuit school he studied [[Ancient Greece|ancient Greece]] and Rome, which led to an appreciation of the Olympics at an early age. He emphasized amateur participation and fair play, and he incorporated arts competitions into the Games. The Pierre de Coubertin Medal is named in his honor.

French magistrate, polymath, and mathematician whose work led to early developments in [[Calculus|infinitesimal calculus]]. He made notable contributions to [[Analytic geometry|analytic geometry]], [[Probability|probability]], [[Optics|optics]], and [[Number theory|number theory]]. He was a lawyer at the parlement of [[Toulouse|Toulouse]], and he held his office as councillor there for the rest of his life. He communicated most of his work in letters to friends, often with little or no proof. His best-known claim, [[Fermat's Last Theorem|Fermat's Last Theorem]], was described in a note in the margin of a copy of Diophantus' *Arithmetica* and was not resolved until 1994. He was also a skilled Latinist and Hellenist, and his priority disputes with contemporaries such as Descartes and Wallis were common.

English journalist and television presenter. [[Rupert Murdoch|Rupert Murdoch]] appointed him editor of the *News of the World* in 1994, at the age of 29, making him the youngest editor of a British national newspaper in more than half a century. He later edited the *Daily Mirror* until 2004. He co-presented ITV's *Good Morning Britain* and in 2008 won *The Celebrity Apprentice* alongside [[Donald Trump]]. His talk show later moved from TalkTV to [[YouTube]]. A 2023 court case found truthful evidence that he knew about private phone hacking from a reporter.

Marble sculpture by [[Michelangelo]] showing Jesus and Mary, carved in 1498–1499 for Saint Peter's Basilica in [[Vatican City]]. It captures the moment Jesus, taken down from the cross, is given to his mother. Mary looks younger than Jesus, and art historians believe Michelangelo was inspired by a passage in [[Dante Alighieri]]'s *Divine Comedy*. It is a key work of Italian [[Renaissance]] sculpture and is often taken as the start of the High Renaissance. Commissioned by a French cardinal for his funeral chapel in Old St Peter's, it was moved to its current location in the 18th century. It is the only piece Michelangelo ever signed. After Mary's figure was vandalized in 1972, the statue was protected by bulletproof glass.

Dutch painter and art theorist, a pioneer of 20th-century [[Abstract art|abstract art]] and a principal contributor to the De Stijl movement, which he co-founded with Theo van Doesburg. Born in Amersfoort, he moved from naturalistic landscapes toward simple geometric elements. He developed a non-representational form he called Neoplasticism, limiting his vocabulary to the three [[Primary color|primary colors]] (red, blue, and yellow), the three primary values (black, white, and gray), and the two primary directions (horizontal and vertical). He moved to Paris in 1912, where he encountered [[Cubism|Cubism]], and he dropped an *a* from the Dutch spelling of his name, Mondriaan. He proclaimed in 1914 that "art should be above reality", and his work was highly utopian, concerned with universal values and aesthetics.

Dutch and Flemish Renaissance painter and printmaker, known for [[Landscape painting|landscapes]] and [[Peasant|peasant]] scenes. He was a pioneer in presenting both types of subject as large paintings. After training and travels to Italy, where he visited [[Rome]] and probably [[Sicily]], he returned in 1555 to settle in [[Antwerp]]. There he worked mainly as a prolific designer of prints. He made painting his main medium at the end of the 1550s, and his famous paintings come from little more than a decade before his early death in 1569. He painted no portraits. Works including *Landscape with the Fall of Icarus* and *The Hunters in the Snow* have inspired artists in literature and cinema.

Electric charge that accumulates in certain solids, such as [[Crystal|crystals]], [[Ceramic|ceramics]], and bone, in response to applied mechanical stress. The effect is reversible: applying an electric field strains the material, which is how [[Ultrasound|ultrasound]] waves are produced. French physicists Jacques and [[Pierre Curie]] discovered it in 1880. It is used in sound detection and production, clock generators in electronic devices, and microbalances. It forms the basis of scanning probe microscopes, and it is used in some electric guitar pickups and as triggers in most modern electronic drums.

Intermediate good with high [[Carbon|carbon]] content, typically 3.8–4.7%, made by smelting [[Iron ore|iron ore]] in a blast furnace. Its brittleness makes it unusable directly, so it is mainly used as feedstock for [[Steel|steel]]. The name comes from the sand molds, in which ingots branched from a central channel, resembling piglets nursing from a sow. It was made in China by the later [[Zhou dynasty|Zhou dynasty]] (ended 256 BC), and the earliest archaeologically confirmed Chinese blast furnaces date to the [[Han dynasty|Han dynasty]]. In Europe, blast furnaces producing pig iron appeared during the [[Middle Ages|Middle Ages]]. Traditionally it was worked into [[Wrought iron|wrought iron]] in forges and puddling furnaces.

Chemical compound used to add or alter color, nearly or completely insoluble in water, unlike [[Dye|dyes]]. Pigments are often inorganic and have been used since prehistoric times, including [[Ochre|ochre]], [[Charcoal|charcoal]], and [[Lapis lazuli|lapis lazuli]]. The first known synthetic pigment, Egyptian blue, was made by heating quartz sand, lime, and a copper source such as [[Malachite|malachite]], and is attested in Egypt circa 3250 BC. Around 7.4 million tons of pigments were marketed worldwide in 2006. The white pigment [[Titanium dioxide|titanium dioxide]] was placed at $13.2 billion per year, and organic pigments are mainly used in printing inks, followed by paints, plastics, and textiles.

Small, tailless mammal of the family Ochotonidae, native to mountains in [[Asia|Asia]] and [[North America|North America]]. Pikas resemble their close relative the [[Rabbit|rabbit]] but have a very round body and short, rounded ears. They prefer rocky slopes and are [[Herbivore|herbivores]] that store hay under rocks for the long, cold winter. Their high-pitched alarm call gives them the nickname whistling [[Hare|hare]]. The genus *Ochotona* covers 37 species. The American pika lives mainly in the mountains of the western United States.

Electric-type [[Pokémon|Pokémon]] species and the mascot of the franchise. Created by Atsuko Nishida at the request of lead designer Ken Sugimori, it first appeared in *Pokémon Red and Blue* on the [[Game Boy|Game Boy]]. It is a large yellow mouse with a lightning bolt-shaped tail and red cheek sacs that generate electricity. It evolves into Raichu after exposure to the Thunder Stone. Pikachu is widely considered the most popular Pokémon species, largely because of its role as the companion of Ash Ketchum in the [[Pokémon (TV series)|anime series]]. Critics have praised its cute design.

Mind-body exercise system named after its developer, Joseph Pilates, who called it "Contrology". It developed in the aftermath of late 19th-century physical culture and is practiced worldwide, especially in [[Australia|Australia]], [[Canada|Canada]], the [[United States|United States]], and the [[United Kingdom|United Kingdom]]. As of 2005 there were 11 million regular practitioners and 14,000 instructors in the United States. Pilates emphasizes core strength, where [[Yoga|yoga]] emphasizes flexibility. Evidence is limited: it improves balance but has not been shown to treat any medical condition, although regular sessions can help muscle conditioning in healthy adults.

Journey to a holy place, often on foot, undertaken for spiritual or moral significance. It may lead to personal transformation before the pilgrim returns to daily life. The word *pilgrim* derives from the Latin *peregrinus*, meaning a traveler from afar. The practice predates Christianity and appears in the faiths of [[Ancient Egypt|ancient Egypt]], India, China, and Japan. The Holy Land is a focal point for [[Judaism|Judaism]], [[Christianity|Christianity]], and [[Islam|Islam]]. In Islam, the [[Hajj|Hajj]] to the [[Kaaba|Kaaba]] is one of the Five Pillars. The [[Kumbh Mela|Kumbh Mela]] in Hinduism is held every twelve years at four sacred river sites, including [[Prayagraj|Prayagraj]].
